utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I ask for the Registrar to call out the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Williamson, Ms. Sutherland, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning, my name is Toma Fila and I am here this morning with my colleagues, Miss Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we will now continue with the expert witness. I wonder whether the Registrar could call the witness -- sorry, the usher. Mr. Fila, I wonder, how much time do you need now to continue your cross-examination of Dr. Wheeler?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Not more than one hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: One hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was hoping that you would need only half an hour, because there are also some questions from the bench and we have two more witnesses. I wonder whether you could try, as much as possible, to reduce the time you need. I mean, of course, it is for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said one hour so that you would not tell me that I have extended the time. I am sure that it will be shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am not going to bother you for a very long time, Dr. Wheeler. Mr. Wheeler, before we start with questions, yesterday you said that all of the Eagles were an organisation that belonged to Seselj. Could it be Bokan, maybe? Seselj's men were Chetniks. I am not trying to impose my opinion, but..

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to admit that I have read both, that (transcript unavailable) Chetnik. One has to admit that in this matter of paramilitaries the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Not that it is terribly important, but -- yes, they were all paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The so-called authorities tend to differ in the accounts they give, and I have not actually myself ever had the dubious privilege of meeting any of these people, other than in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, Bokan was in prison and Seselj, no. Yesterday you said that the first conflict in the territory of Vukovar began with the incident in Borovo Selo. Do you know anything about who killed -- who murdered Reichl Kir, police chief for the territory of Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of his own younger officers shot him as he sat in his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat. A young Croat who apparently had just lost his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did that cause tensions in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly an awful lot of outsiders who have written about it agree that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And those people, did they try to accuse Serbs for that crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly in the western press at the time it took place, local accusations against the Serbs existed. Subsequently, of course, everybody knows the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You saw probably on TV, "Death of Yugoslavia", a BBC programme, and the interview that took place with his wife. Do you remember that Kir's wife said that before the attack on the Serbian policemen on Borovo Selo there had been a provocation. Certain people, shot on the village. That was shown on your television, on the British television. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, so does that mean that there were provocations on the part of Croats before Serbs actually killed those policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were provocations on both sides. Certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I did not ask about both sides, I just ask you whether Croats did any provocations. Mr. Niemann will probably ask you about Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness might be permitted to answer fully to the question, your Honour, when asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. Nothing against him answering the question, I just wanted to know whether Croats did any provocations in Borovo Selo before the incident took place, and I wanted a yes or no answer, and if I am not mistaken, the answer was, "yes".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right. The answer is "yes", and I said as much, of course, in the written statement I submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is okay. Did an expulsion of Serbs take place from the territory of Vukovar before August 1991 and do you know how many left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many left. I have seen various figures. I do not know anything about their accuracy, but before August of 1991 most of these departures on the part of Serbs I do not think can actually be described as, "expulsions". The level of tension was very great, and people were fleeing. Serbs were fleeing, as were Croats. They felt in many cases that the situation was such that they were leaving under pressure, but I do not think you could describe it as "ethnic cleansing" in the way that term later became understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, of course not. I did not mean to say that. The question followed the issue of mistrust, mutual mistrust. I did not mean it as ethnic cleansing. In Vukovar, was there a JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there -- throughout Croatia, military installations were under blockade, the electricity was cut off, water supply as well, before August 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly President Tudjman's decision to embrace the blockade of JNA barracks as a military tactic came that summer. I do not actually know whether before August of 1991 any barracks were under blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You do not know at all whether there were any blockades -- you know, for example, about Split.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On 6th May 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The blockade of barracks had been used by as a general Croatian strategy. I believe it actually started in August, where it became widespread. Virtually all barracks being blockaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whether there were any soldiers, young soldiers, conscripts doing their military service in those barracks at that time, soldiers coming from all parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I mean, the effectiveness of that as a strategy on the part of the Croats depended upon -- that is a strategy dependent upon, of course, their having hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, not only Serbs were in those barracks. That is the essence of my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The one who was strangled in Split near the tank, was he a Serb or a Macedonian? You know the incident I am referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. A Macedonian. Was there a decision of the presidency of the SFRY headed by Stipe Mesic, therefore a presidency in full composition, about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a decision, decisions of the presidency of Yugoslav that were reached by all members of the presidency on the disarmament and dissolution of paramilitary formations? Those decisions were brought in the first half of 1991 and were signed by Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the presidency agreed that paramilitary formations should be abolished, but of course, this did not include Serb paramilitary formations in Croatia at the time, and of course, as you well know, the decision was not carried out. Tudjman managed to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether there was a decision signed by a Croat. That was my question. Do you know that there was a decision issued by the Croatian Parliament of 5th December 1991 on the withdrawal of all Croatian representatives from the federal administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. I just want to mention that that decision has been handed over to you, and the Prosecution has disputed its authenticity. You have shown, and that is a Prosecution exhibit number 1, an ethnic map of Yugoslavia from 1991. You remember exhibit number 1. Do you remember it? This is the map I am referring to. Would you kindly show the court how many Serbs lived there and how many remain -- how many Serbs remain today in Croatia on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are there any Serbs in Lika, Kordun, Banija, northern Dalmatia? Is there any Serb living there, except for elderly people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are very few Serbs living there now, after Oluja and Bljesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is there a single military-aged man living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are, some have returned, especially from Eastern Slavonia, in the past year or so, but immediately after Oluja, the Serb population of then UN sectors north and south or the former sectors north and south was reduced to below 10,000 persons. Between 8 and 10,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Which political group was supported by the extremist Ustasha immigration, HDZ or STP, whose member Dokmanovic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it qualifies as a leading question. Obviously, insofar as there were extreme nationalist Croats abroad who owed some sort of family or ideological legacy to the Ustasha immigration of the immediate post-Second World War period, they would have tended to favour the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there today in the Croatian Parliament, are there any descendants from that Ustasha organisation? Where is Gojka Susak from, the Minister of Defence of Croatia? Does he come from the immigration circles? From Canada? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is the author of the book, the original title is "Bespvce Povijesne Zbilje"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the condition for recognition of Croatia by Israel a public apology from Mr. Tudjman, from President Tudjman for his anti-semitic allegations in that book? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but would I not be surprised if the answer is, "yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Croatia have some kind of Willy Brandt in its history after the Second World War, to apologise, the way Willy Brandt did, to all of the victims that were killed in the Jasenovac camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly there was no charismatic political leader who took upon himself that role, although I think in practical terms one might actually have thought that Vladimir Bakaric had some sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Communist era. That would conclude my questions concerning JNA and the political situation. With your permission, your Honours, I would ask just a couple of questions regarding the local government. Let us finish with these bloody issues. Let us talk about something else. You said yesterday that you are familiar with the constitutional order of Yugoslavia. Which unit of the local government is the principal unit in Yugoslavia? Is that the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the municipality, the "opstina", made up of "mesadijnes", or local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, and so on. What is the role of any parliamentary body, parliamentary authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the role of any assembly, any representative assembly, of course, is the legislative function.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is right. The municipality upwards, the republic, the state, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. President of the municipal assembly -- I am sorry, let me rephrase it. Within the municipal assembly -- I am trying to speed up the proceedings -- is there an executive council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does it constitute the executive authority on the territory of that municipality? Does it have its own president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have a chairman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the president of the municipal assembly reach independent decisions, any decision apart from a convening session of the assembly itself? Represent the assembly to sign decisions that were passed by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the system of municipal government was that of a hybrid one. The president of the local assembly would have executive powers and certainly would have authority because of the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The president of the executive council, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the president of the assembly also would have certain executive authority, in practice if not in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In theory, I am asking, because in practise, yes, it may be that the person who enjoys the highest reputation in the area. Now, please let us clarify something because of various rumours. Does the municipal assembly or its president appoint judges, prosecutors, does he conduct trials in any way? Or is this the judiciary that has nothing to do with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that you are correct in suggesting it has nothing to do with him. It is a matter for the judicial --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does he appear as commander of military barracks? Does he have some kind of authority over military units stationed on the territory of his municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the Territorial Defence system, in certain circumstances the local authorities collectively would have influence over that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking about the JNA. The JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over the JNA, over the People's Army? No. But over Territorial Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking about the JNA. That is what I am interested in. Does the witness know that on the territory of the SFRY there were also military courts. Does the president to the municipal assembly have certain competencies, jurisdiction as regards military courts? Because he did not have any other civilian courts, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly in theory he ought not to have any such competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does the president of the municipal assembly appoint the Chief of Police or is this done by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, in theory, no. In practice, certainly this would be something in which the influence, the, "fazir", of the President of the Assembly or any other high ranking local person often would be brought to bear. In other words, the local assembly chief could easily pick up the telephone and talk to the Minister of the Interior in the republican capital and get his man --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is okay. My direct question was in respect of theory and competencies, whether this person could appoint such people or not. I think that we were all agreed that the president of the municipal assembly is the first person in town, the topmost important in the town. In a situation of war or of immediate threat of war, does his position change in respect of the JNA? For example, if war breaks out, can this person command over the JNA? Does this person have command over the JNA if there is an internal or international conflict or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but if there were an international conflict --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking about the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would not have authority over the JNA but over the committee established in which such a person would participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Professor, local crisis staff certainly could not command the JNA, I am just asking about the JNA directly because in this conflict it was the JNA that bombed Vukovar, that shelled Vukovar, not the municipal crisis staff or assembly. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but there would be liaison between the local authorities and the JNA. That certainly would have been provided for. Official liaison.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And to conclude, how does someone become president of the municipal assembly, and how is someone relieved of that duty? Can someone be president of the municipal assembly if the assembly itself has been dissolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the assembly has been dissolved, then no. Any such person could resign or be sacked by his colleagues or in times of extreme danger, of course, the republican authorities in the capital could sack him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I agree with you on that, but we have agreed that if there is not a municipal assembly there is no president of the municipal assembly. Right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unless, of course, a large part of that municipal assembly split off and operated in completely new circumstances outside the prevailing system. I think what you are getting at, of course, is the fact that it could be argued that the Serbian component of the municipal assembly in Vukovar, in particular, at some point in the spring of 1991, ceased to recognise the authority of the Croatian Republic, whereas, of course, the Croatian Republic from Zagreb, of course, was seeking to disband the municipal assembly in Vukovar, so there was a mutual disrecognition that took place in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they make an attempt to do it or should I show you a document proving that they actually did it, and that they appointed a different person to that same office and this person is going to be a witness here, Belije, and I can show you a document proving that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are correct, indeed. Zagreb did do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Fila. I wonder whether the Prosecutor wants to re-examine the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Wheeler, yesterday you were asked some questions about the role of the JNA, especially in Vukovar, but in other places. After the JNA withdrew from Slovenia in July 1991, could it be said that thereafter it was still fighting to maintain the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in general terms, no. The certainly commanding heights of the JNA had, after the humiliation of the adventure in Slovenia, no place to go other than total allegiance to the lesser aims and objectives of Slobodan Milosevic, but that does not mean that there were still elements in the JNA who continued to believe that they were fighting for Yugoslavia or something, as much of a Yugoslavia as they could have, but they were being increasingly marginalised in terms of influence within the military command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So to some extent are you saying that after that time it then began, by a gradual process, to begin fighting for the Serb state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This process had been a long time in developing, but certainly, I think, the defining moment when the JNA ceases to be an army which represents a vanished state can be dated to the 27th June 1991, when they moved into Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also were asked some questions about the SANU Memorandum and the fact that it was not officially published. At the time that it was produced, would it have been in accord with the Communist ideal of Tito's Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The significance of the SANU Memorandum is that the reaction to it, the popular reaction to it. The mere fact that so many established intellectuals were reacting so negatively towards the Titoist legacy was to show the Communist authorities that they needed a new source of legitimacy. In other words, the SANU Memorandum paved the way for the new ideology of populist nationalism which would allow Slobodan Milosevic in particular to maintain power in Serbia, even though he had jettisoned the old Marxist Leninism. It was a transitional document showing that there was a new source of legitimacy out there to be grabbed and Milosevic eventually grabbed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have an objection, your Honour. The Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, is speculating. No one ever said, "the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts", but only, "the draft memorandum", because a memorandum would be an official document whereas a draft memorandum which was stolen may be a document for someone else but it is certainly not a document for me and that is where the difference is, and the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, is asking about the SANU Memorandum is something which does not exist. That was said yesterday, so this is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we are to be politically correct in terms of Serbian politics, your Honour, I am happy for it to be called, "draft". Dr. Wheeler, in your opinion, did the SFRY cease to exist when Stipe Mesic did not rotate as the SFRY president on 15th May 1991, or do you think that it may have happened earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that one could, in retrospect, identify any number of dates between 1989 and June of 1991, when the SFRY ceased to exist. The 15th May when Mesic was prevented from fulfilling the chair of the presidency is one possible date. I do not think myself that all bets were off and all hope extinguished that some new form of Yugoslavia might have emerged until shots were exchanged between the JNA and the Slovene forces in June. I think that was the point of absolute no return, but a constitutionally-minded scholar might well conclude that the 15th May was significant, equally significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During your cross-examination, you were asked questions about fears that Serbs had in 1990 related to what happened at Jasenovac during World War II. Were these fears in any way promoted from Belgrade, Belgrade media or political pronouncements from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, they certainly were. The promotion of fear had been one of the principal planks of Milosevic's policy, since coming to power in Serbia in 1987. The initial objects of Serb terror were meant to be, of course, rampaging Albanian sodomites in Kosovo, who were meant to be going around looking for every Serb nun that they could injure. Later on, the targets expanded into Islamic fundamentalists in Bosnia and the descendants of the Ustashe, or literal Ustashe knife-wielding terrorists in Croatia. This was all part and parcel of Serbian policy at the time, Milosevic's policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were also asked how many Serbs lived -- now live in the Krajina region and you indicated that there are very few there. When did this occur, when did the rapid decline in numbers occur? What year? As a consequence of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, well, the near total extinction of centuries of Serbian habitation in Croatia came in 1995 with the Croatian military actions, Oluja in August and Bljesak in May. A point that I think is important that should be made, however, was that the -- even in the days of its supposed strength, the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina was haemorrhaging people. The population, for economic reasons, because of lack of security, because of the fact it was effectively a gangster state, the population was flowing out from 1991 onwards, but certainly the great mass expulsion, or the great mass flight which could be viewed as an expulsion on the part of the Croatian authorities, took place in the spring and summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just between the period I think you have just touched on, I think between 1991 and 1995, were there many Croats living in this region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had long since been cleansed, in the same way that Mr. Fila pointed out, the bulk of the remaining Serbian population in these former Serb-ruled areas is elderly, so too, before 1995, the remaining Croats in Serb-controlled areas were also simply the elderly, the people who had no option but to stay put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this cleansing of the Croats, that occurred in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it began in 1990 and continued through 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. I thought that Mr. Niemann had completed his examination. We know that we all have the same rights, so if he put further questions, then I am entitled to do the same thing. Yesterday, the expert said that it was a draft memorandum, and that it was stolen from the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. Is that true or not? Because someone has misspoken, either I or Mr. Niemann. Is it an official document of the SANU order, or is it a draft that was stolen from the SANU, so it is a very clear question, we should clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, just one question because under our Rules of Procedure, Rule 85(B), only examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination shall be allowed in each case, so for the sake of clarifying this matter I will allow you to ask just one question and then we will move on to the questions from the bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the expert witness to reply, to answer this question? Did you ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila is correct, it was a draft memorandum, which was purloined, but I think that in retrospect it would be fair to say that it was floated as a trial balloon. In other words, at the time it was far too subversive a document for the official SANU members to be associated with, but they were interested certainly in gauging popular reaction to it. But it was indeed a draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, that is the first part of the question that was answered. The second part is, "was this an official SANU document? An official document of the Serbian Academy of Science and Arts?", so it is one question; was it an official document or a draft that was purloined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Fila is technically correct. It was a draft, it was stolen, and it was not official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We will now move to questions from the bench. Judge May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, you have just been asked about the municipal assembly, and I think that certainly from my point of view it would be helpful to know what the structure of local government was, where the municipal assembly fitted in in Yugoslavia or where, whatever, in 1991 in the early part that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you will have heard me make distinctions between theory and practice in attempting to answer Mr. Fila's questions. The problem was that the structure of local government, like the structure of everything in Yugoslavia after 1974, and the apotheosis of self-management in the constitution of that year, is extremely complex. Everybody was supposed to be meeting all the time with everybody else to establish everything. It was meant to be the world's most thoroughly democratised system, in which everybody, wearing one sort of hat or another, a hat as a producer, a hat as a consumer, a hat as a member of a political -- socio-political organisation, was constantly meeting in assemblies to decide their own affairs. A latter-day cynic would say that this was simply a means of atomising society in order better to guarantee the rule of the party, and it might have worked out that way had the party itself maintained any kind of cohesion or unity, but since the party did not, after Tito's death, since the party was fracturing, so too did the system of -- remember, the system of local government is mirrored in the economy, it is mirrored in the way in which the forces of law and order are supposedly managed, everybody is involved in this self-management system of endless assemblies and endless meetings. In point of fact, therefore, when the cohesion is gone, after Tito, the system really rather breaks down and we have to start talking about practice rather than theory. So, if you would like to try to pose a specific question to me about how it may have worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what I want to know is what is the municipal assembly, then, as a specific question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal assembly would be the equivalent to a city council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the role of the president in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I tried to say to Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Slow down, I think, slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you to slow down, or am I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role of the assembly, the role of the president to the assembly, would depend very much on the authority of the individual, I think. Some individuals would have had a commanding presence and could have run their local districts, their cities, as sort of old-fashioned party bosses. Others would have been creatures of various interest groups and factions, so I do not think it is possible to generalise across any one republic, or certainly across the country as a whole about how powerful a person a president of a local assembly would be. It would depend on that person, and their own power base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who, then, appointed the municipal assembly, who appointed the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, they were elected in elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One party elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Wheeler, I have two questions. Question number 1: in the period between June and September 1991, did the central authorities of Croatia exercise effective control over what has now become the Croatian territory? Were there areas of Croatia that were not under the effective control of the central authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were large areas of Croatia which were outside the control of the capital, outside of Zagreb's control, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Which ones? Could you point to particular areas where there was no effective control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Zagreb's writ did not run in northern Dalmatia, an area around Knin, Zagreb's authority did not prevail in the area to the north of that, Lika and Kordun, and then spreading across the bottom of Croatia, south of Zagreb, in Banija. In the course of that summer further areas exempt themselves from Zagreb's control; latterly, of course, the area that this court is most concerned with, Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In those areas where the central Croatian authorities did exercise effective control, what sort of control did they exercise? I mean, in other words, this control, what sort of manifestations took up? I mean, say, military control? Administrative control? Economic control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all of those ways. The Tudjman government, when it was elected in April and May of 1990, had very grand ambitions for restoring what they saw as Croatian authority in Croatia itself. There was a feeling on the part of many Croatian nationalists that their country, their Republic had, for too long, been ruled by alien elements, whether those were Communists or Serbs or the products of mixed marriages or all sorts of dubious elements, in any case, and there was a determination on the part of Tudjman to get rid of the Communists, and to get rid of the Serbs. That meant imposing his own people in the judiciary, in the press, in the media, in the police, all of those areas which were vital for the assurgence of the new party's control. This, of course, would be an aim of any incoming government where one party replaces another, but after 40-some years of Communist rule, and given the nationalistic tenor of the times, the purge, if one could call it that, was destined to be more extreme in Croatia, than it would, for example, be in the United States when a Republican administration replaces a Democratic administration. There is of course a purge in both cases, but the extent of that purge was, of course, in the Croatian circumstance, all the greater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on to my second. Question: in the armed conflict that broke out in Eastern Slavonia in 1991, were the local Serbian civilians fighting against the Croatian authorities integrated into the JNA, or did they make up a separate body of combatants independent of the JNA? When I speak of Serbian civilians I intend to refer to persons not belonging to the paramilitary units, such as those led by Arkan and Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, many local civilians would have joined or formed their own paramilitary units which would have worked hand in glove with the JNA. The extent to which residual Serbian civilian authorities worked with the JNA, if that is what you are asking, would have, I suppose, varied according to the effectiveness of the local liaison which was established by both sides. We know, for example, in the case of the Knin area, where much more has been written about this, that the intensity or intimacy of the co-operation between local Serbian authorities and the military varied tremendously depending on the personalities involved. I would imagine that in Western or Eastern Slavonia, that this would have been the same, that in some places, again, the local authorities that remained or were acting in defiance of Zagreb were totally integrated with, and collaborating with the JNA. In other areas, perhaps this could have been from village to village, almost. They could have been rather more independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there is any objection to Dr. Wheeler being released. Any objection from the Prosecutor or from the Defence? (Pause). All right, so you may be released, Dr. Wheeler, thank you so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Borislav Magovac. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Magovac. Could you please make the solemn declaration? BORISLAV MAGOVAC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Magovac, would you state your full name for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Borislav Magovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 23rd August 1950 in Brodski Stupnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you later become a professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I completed my university studies in the former Yugoslavia I had to pass an examination to become a professor at secondary school and that is what I did, and I became a professor of Marxism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you live for the most part of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I permanently lived in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you very briefly just outline your professional career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After finishing my university studies I started teaching in a secondary school in Backa Palanka as a professor. After that, after seven years in Backa Palanka I became director of the kindergarten in Ilok, and I spent about four years there and after that I was appointed director of the catering company in Vukovar until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you stop working in Vukovar and why did you stop working in Vukovar, the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped working in Vukovar on 23rd August 1991. I know the exact date because it was my birthday. I was unable to continue working in Vukovar due to the very difficult and complex situation. War operations had started against the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you stopped working in Vukovar, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on with my life in Ilok. With a group of citizens of Ilok we established a body which started working on the overall organisation of life and activities in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the main function of this organisation? What was its primary objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This party was established by the municipal assembly of Ilok because of the exceptionally difficult and complex situation. In terms of the overall organisation of life in the area, an executive body was necessary in order to coordinate various agreements between us and the neighbouring town of Backa Palanka and Sid, and having a good relationship, or rather some kind of working relationship with both, was essential to our survival at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Backa Palanka and Sid, are those towns both in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Say in Serbia, yes, but at that time it was the autonomous province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why was it necessary to try and establish good relations with both those towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you are familiar with the geo-strategic position of the town of Ilok. Then you can see that it deeply penetrates the territory of the Republic of Serbia and the only possible contact with Croatia is via Vukovar, or rather Tovarnik. Once this was cut off the only way to survive was to have some kind of communication between these towns, between which the town of Ilok is located anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have lost the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Because of technical problems I propose we have a recess of 15 minutes. (9:45 am) (A short break) (9:50 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Magovac, could you please briefly describe for their Honours the build-up of tension in the Ilok area in particular, but in the region around Ilok in 1991, in a brief sort of description of the build-up of tensions in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More significant disturbances or tensions took place after the conflict in Borovo Selo and after the death of a certain number of members of MUP in the summer of 1991. The situation was getting more complex every day, in all aspects of everyday life, but the climax was the situation got really unbearable after the direct attacks and after the start of military operations in the area of Vukovar. Ilok is situated 35 kilometres east of Vukovar, and by way of comparison, let me say that it is a kind of dead-end of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and all routes, all communication lines were cut off from the direction of Vukovar. Therefore, this kind of situation affected the organisation of everyday life. Let me mention, perhaps, a banal detail. A simple aspirin was almost impossible to obtain, let alone problems with electricity, water supply, and so on. The supply of the city itself, and its citizens, became a very big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who was responsible for cutting Vukovar off from its lines of supply? Who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilok, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, from Vukovar. I think you said it had lines of supply from Vukovar, but perhaps generally. Its lines of supply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that the supply, lines of supply were interrupted, were cut off by the JNA that took, at the end of the month of August, all key positions around the town of Ilok. For example, the road towards Sid, Backa Palanka, the road leading to the bridge, and so on. Also, due to the military operations in the area of Vukovar at that time, it was impossible to travel in that direction. It was impossible to have any kind of contact with the rest of Croatia. At that time at the end of August, the JNA occupied all key positions, strategic positions, strategic points in the area of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In Ilok itself, who was opposing the JNA, if anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the opposition opposing the JNA in Ilok was none. There had been some kind of attempt to negotiate in Ilok. We tried to negotiate with the representatives of the JNA, and we also attempted to prevent the JNA from entering Ilok and occupying the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about in other parts of the municipality of Vukovar? Do you know who it was that was opposing the JNA in those other parts of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the manager of a catering company I had entered into some contracts -- I signed a contract with the Ministry of the Interior. The contract related to the accommodation and provisions, supplies for the Ministry of the Interior. I also signed a contract with the Croatian guards, Croatian National Guards, an agreement about the same type of services that I provided to the Ministry of the Interior. Therefore, officially those who did resist the JNA at that time -- I am referring to the period at the end of August -- where members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia and members of the Croatian National Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by, "members of the Ministry of the Interior", that is the police is it,?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the National Guard of Croatia was referred to as the ZNG. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you just -- now, you mentioned earlier that you were on this executive body of Ilok that was appointed by the Ilok assembly. Can you describe for me the structure of local government in that part of Yugoslavia at the time, as it applied to the town of Ilok? Can you tell me how the structure worked in Ilok town itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as structure and organisation is concerned, Ilok had a kind of local government. The local government in Ilok was structured in the following way; there were four local communes and because of the town itself and the way it was organised, those four local communes entered a kind of assembly or a community, and the principal body of that community was the assembly of the town. The assembly elected its own executive council, town council, as an executive body. Among other executive bodies, the assembly was able to establish various commissions or committees, and let me just mention, for example, that when certain works had to be carried out, like harvest, for example, at the level of the town municipal assembly, we would usually establish a commission that took care of all problems concerning the harvest, protection against fire and so on. Also, whenever circumstances were very difficult, and especially in view of the very difficult situation at the end of the month of August, the assembly decided --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I interrupted you. We had some trouble with the screen. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of August, due to a very complex situation which had befallen the town of Ilok, the town assembly established one more body, namely a commission which was tasked with establishing contacts, conducting negotiations with the neighbouring town of Backa Palanka, members or representatives of the JNA and representatives of the town of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were appointed to this commission, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the purpose of it was to meet with Serb representatives, was it not, including the JNA, and civil people in civil authority in order to try and resolve the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was asking you some questions about the town assembly. The town assembly, you said, appointed an executive council. Was a president also appointed to the town assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what of the executive council? Was there an executive council of Ilok? -- sorry, I withdraw that. With respect to the executive council, did it also appoint a president, or was that president the same one as the town assembly president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President of the executive council was a special office, special importance. It is an executive body of the town assembly, and of course, it demanded a special function. The president of the executive council was Mr. Crvenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Ilok is in the municipality of Vukovar, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And there is an assembly for the municipality as well, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is the assembly for the municipality in a higher position than the assembly for the town, say, for example, of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is the -- did the town of Vukovar itself also have a town assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town of Vukovar had several local communes, but there was no assembly of local communes. Each local commune was represented at territorial hall, and this was something specific for that area. Local communes had the statutes of small towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the -- can you tell us what, if any, was the relationship between the local administration at Ilok and the municipal administration of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The everyday life of the citizens of the former Yugoslavia and the fulfilment of their everyday needs was carried out, realised, and implemented at the level of municipality. In the political system of the SFRY, municipality represented a kind of base for the fulfilment of everyday needs of the citizens of Yugoslavia. As far as more specific, immediate needs of the citizens were concerned, there was lower level as well, namely local communes. Local communes were lower bodies, lower types of organisations which were meant to provide for the needs of the local population. The idea was to have this process of making decisions concerning everyday life of citizens as close as possible to the local population. Therefore, we had a number of local communes in our territory, almost every single village was a local commune within the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what was the highest position, the highest position one could reach in the whole of the municipality? What position was the highest position in the municipality in local government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The highest body, authority, the highest authority was the municipal assembly. At that time, municipal assemblies had their own executive bodies that were tasked with carrying out its main functions. The principal organ, therefore, was the municipal assembly which was formed, appointed through elections. The population would choose their deputies, their representatives to the municipal assembly and in that way the municipal assembly would represent all the citizens of the territory concerned, and here we are speaking about the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what about the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the assembly, municipal assembly, was first of all a delegate of the assembly who was then elected by other members of the assembly, other delegates, and he was responsible for conducting the affairs and the work of the municipality, and to act through various municipal executive bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in these proceedings, Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And for how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew each other since my arrival in Vukovar, when I was appointed director of the catering company. We had contact very often, but I could not tell you exactly the day we were introduced, we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in the early part of 1991 do you know what position the accused had in local government, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the elections that took place in 1991, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic became a member of the assembly and as a delegate of the assembly he was elected president of the municipal assembly, president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And just to make it clear, I think you have probably done so, but just to make it clear, the president of the municipality is a higher position in the hierarchy of local government than a president of the town assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. But let me just clarify, if I may, once again. I would like to explain the way the local government was structured in Vukovar. Vukovar comprised several local communes, as I have already pointed out, but these local communes did not form a so-called community of local communes, and they did not have -- they did not form a kind of city council. Therefore, the town of Vukovar only had a municipal assembly. There were several assemblies of local communes, and there was no town assembly. The town of Vukovar did not have a town assembly. It only had a municipal assembly for the whole territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the person that you know as Slavko Dokmanovic in court today? Can you see him in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you please point to him and describe where he is sitting the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic is sitting left, on my left side. I do not know how else I can describe him. He is sitting next to the wall. Is this enough, as identification? He has a moustache. His hair is a bit more white than it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough. What is the relationship, if any, the official relationship, if any, between the president of a municipality and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the municipality is the representative of all citizens of the municipality. He is a civilian, and the relationship between the president of the municipality and the JNA can be described, can be only through one body of the municipality, and at that time, that was the secretariat for the national defence. It was some kind of link between the civilian side, between civilian authorities and the JNA. Otherwise, a direct relationship, a direct link in terms of political bodies and functions, I can only mention maybe certain bodies that existed within the Communist party. For example, the president of the municipality was a civilian representative of the citizens and he did not belong to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could the president, for example -- could the president of the municipality actually give any orders to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The JNA had its own law on the national defence, and the structure of the government simply did not allow for the president of the municipality to issue any kind of orders to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the president of the municipality and Territorial Defence? Was there any official relationship between those two positions or bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since according to the law on the national defence in the former Yugoslavia, a concept of an armed population, armed people was established. One of the components of that idea of that concept was that organisation of the Territorial Defence. Territorial Defence was responsible to the secretariat of the national -- for the national defence, and the civilian side, civilian authorities had more influence on the Territorial Defence in terms of its structure, organisation, financial support, as well as training, and so on. Training of the Territorial Defence in case of war emergencies, and so on, and other potential problems, problems that could arise on the territory of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did the president of the municipality in certain circumstances have the authority to mobilise local defence? The Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He could, in case of major disasters, in case of immediate threat of various kinds of dangers, I cannot right now be more specific. I do not remember what else was provided for by the law, but yes, he could mobilise the Territorial Defence for the purpose of alleviating the situation in all kinds of emergencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And those are more in the nature of civil defence such as earthquakes, floods, civil disobedience and things of that nature. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And insofar as he was able to mobilise them for those purposes, did he have authority over them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At any rate, he was president of the municipality, and he had legal powers to conduct affairs concerning the Territorial Defence and one of the key functions of the president of the municipality was related to the Territorial Defence as far as the former Yugoslavia was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if I could take you back to the events in Ilok that you started to describe for us earlier in your evidence, by the time that the JNA began surrounding Ilok, displaced persons began to congregate in this town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, let me say, let me remind you that Ilok is the easternmost point of the Republic of Croatia. You should not forget that there was a very important route, a very important communication line, Vukovar, Sotin, Sid, which historically was known as the front of "Srem". It is a very important area in geo-strategical sense, it was a very important road which was important not only in these recent events, but throughout history. The villages alongside this line, this particular road, were Croatian villages. I can quickly enumerate them. Let me start with Opatovac, Mohovo, Sarengrad, Lovas, Bapska. When the line was disrupted, and when the only way for them to function, because the line was disrupted by the JNA, the JNA did not want to have any problems alongside that line, so the majority of residents, the majority of citizens of that area, especially after the fall of Tovarnik -- I want to say that the only place where they could come to, where they could go, was the town of Ilok, so under the pressure of the JNA they were withdrawing in the direction of Ilok, and let me say that at that time it was the only free enclave which provided a minimal safety for those people. So, the town of Ilok was their last resort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, was it when these refugees came to Ilok that your negotiations as part of the commission for negotiations, is that when it began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started negotiating earlier, but after the arrival of the displaced persons from the surrounding villages, there were circumstances which were already very difficult in town, became even worse. Here I am referring to the problems of accommodation, food, and the most basic life necessities, because at that time the town of Ilok, within the period of several days, the population of the town of Ilok doubled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you had your negotiations, who did you negotiate with on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The negotiations were conducted with two sides. We negotiated with military authorities, but we also had talks and negotiations with civilian representatives from the neighbouring town of Backa Palanka, as well as Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what positions did these civilian persons hold, that you negotiated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the representatives of Backa Palanka and Sid, or to our specific position in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Backa Palanka and Sid. I am asking who was representing those two areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should know that my involvement, my participation in the commission of the town of Ilok was motivated by my friendship with a number of people from Ilok and elsewhere. I was a professor in the town of Ilok, and, thanks to my long-term experience, I had a very wide circle of acquaintances and friends and through the contacts with the representatives of Backa Palanka, therefore, thanks, as I say, to our previous work and contacts, I was able to have contacts with people who were very respected persons in Backa Palanka. Here I am referring to the president of the SPS, who was my school colleague, and who was also a professor of Marxism, and we used to work together. The role and the importance of the president of the SPS was very great at that moment. It still is, even to the present day. And then through him and because I knew some other people personally, for example, the president of the executive council of Backa Palanka and other people as well, we were able to establish contacts with the highest level representatives of the town of Backa Palanka, in a very direct way. However, bearing in mind that it was in the SFRY, lots of talks were carried out at the level of local communes. Let me mention the name of one of that local commune, Petar Drapsin, which was situated near the bridge in the area called Kalos. That particular local area was linked in a very immediate way with the town of Ilok. So we conducted talks at the level of the local commune and the representatives of the local commune, but we also conducted negotiations at the highest level of the municipality. We had contacts with the president of the municipality, president of the executive council, and the president of the SPS of Backa Palanka, which at that time was the strongest political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of these negotiations that you had, did the Serbian side ever request the presence of a civil authority from Vukovar? Did at any time this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubo Novakovic, during the contacts we had with him, he requested that our interests be represented by Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the man, the gentleman that you have mentioned, was he president -- the person that requested the presence of Mr. Dokmanovic, what position did he hold in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was president of the municipality of Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic take part in these meetings, in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You must be aware of the fact that at that time it was our assessment from Ilok that any interference of Vukovar in the case and position, so to speak, of Ilok would impede negotiations and make our position more difficult. Therefore, from the very outset we built a concept and strategy of defending the fate of the citizens of Ilok and the town of Ilok by ourselves, that we are wise enough, capable enough, of handling the situation in all its complexity, in contacts with the representatives of Backa Palanka in Sid, and I must say that ultimately this proved to be the right thing to do. And I should say that regardless of the way in which all of this happened, we nevertheless played the game to the very end, relying upon our own resources without anybody's help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall a particular meeting at Sid when the meeting was interrupted and you were taken to a headquarters of a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that there were several meetings in Sid. One of the meetings that you are reminding me of was held at highest possible level, speaking in local terms. This meeting started at the assembly of the town of Sid under the chairmanship of the president of the assembly of the town of Sid. This meeting was also attended by the president of the assembly of Backa Palanka, and, because it was held at our request, four representatives of the town of Ilok were there, and among the four, I was one of the representatives, too. After a one-hour discussion in the town assembly somebody walked into the office of the president of the assembly of the town of Sid. This person was wearing a uniform, and this person asked for this meeting with us, the representatives of Ilok, to be interrupted, that we should cross the street from the assembly, because that is where "Radio Sid" was, and probably is until the present day, and on the third or fourth floor of the building at that time, that is to say September 1991, that is where the headquarters of the units we called, "Chetnik units", were. They had their insignia up there, and we who are a bit familiar with this history recognised them to be the White Eagles, "berlij orlovi".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you describe the uniform of the White Eagles that the people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their uniform, if that is what one calls a uniform, was black attire, and the patches were this big (indicating), metal patches with two eagles, one next to the other, and we called them the "White Eagles".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, do you know who the overall leader of the White Eagles in Serbia was at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who commanded them from a military point of view, but the political advocate of this movement, until the present day, is Mr. Seselj, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you when you went to the headquarters of the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I do not know why the presidents allowed this meeting at the assembly to be interrupted. Secondly, I must say quite frankly that without any false accusations by these military units -- actually, I do not understand what the purpose of their interruption of this attempt to have the civilian authorities meet was meant to be directed at. They tried to intimidate us. They tried to cause a psychosis with unreasonable accusations, and I say this quite responsibly, as far as the citizens of Ilok are concerned, because this certainly could not pertain to them. So, they tried to demonstrate their supremacy, their power. They tried to intimidate us, and finally the meeting ended at their headquarters without any conclusions. Just as they had abruptly interrupted our meeting, after a long exposé‚ and pretended concern about the situation in Ilok, they consulted between themselves briefly and they abruptly ended the whole meeting in the same way. The point of the meeting was not there. That is not why we had met. I believed then, and I believe today, that the only purpose of this was to intimidate us and to try to extort some kind of confession from the citizens of Ilok, that they had done something which they certainly had not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after this particular meeting did you have another meeting with the civil representatives of Sid and Backa Palanka, and at that meeting were representatives of the JNA present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meetings were held practically every day. It is not only one meeting that was held. Several meetings were held, both in Backa Palanka as well as in Sid. According to our needs, and depending on the questions that we were supposed to resolve, the representatives of the JNA were included in these meetings, both in Backa Palanka and in Sid, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who represented the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that officially, as far as Ilok is concerned, the JNA was represented by Colonel Grahovac, and I think that he was responsible to General Arandelovic, and the General had his headquarters in Sid, and his command post was in the Red Cross building in Sid, and that is where we had several meetings, rather negotiations on all problems related to our life and the problems we had in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, towards the end of the negotiations that you had, did you obtain, or did you ascertain what the representatives of -- the civilian representatives and what the JNA wanted from the people of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I think that the representatives of the civilian authorities and the representatives of the JNA were harbouring a major delusion as far as Ilok is concerned, especially its degree of organisation, its military power, and various potentials, and they had feared this to a certain extent. Probably because of certain failures they had at Vukovar and also the major losses they had at Vukovar, I think that it was their assessment, and it was certainly wrong that we in Ilok had, I do not know what kind of weapons, so I must say that at all meetings, they insinuated, they made insinuations and they asked us about things that we simply did not have, and on the other hand, they asked for a direct surrender of the citizens of Ilok, namely that they would take over the government in Ilok, and that they would leave us all our rights, namely that nothing would happen to us. So, every meeting was a kind of accusation. Namely, that we had major arms, and also that we should simply surrender and that we should surrender all the arms we had to them. In order to understand this better I am saying clearly and with full responsibility, that to the best of my knowledge, and I think that I was quite involved, and that I think I am quite familiar with the military arsenal that the citizens of Ilok had, I am saying that they only had personal weapons, so to speak and when I say, "personal weapons", I mean pistols, rifles, and some kind of mines. We tried to make them by hand so that we could defend ourselves, protect ourselves, but I think that they were so destructive, even for ourselves, that you cannot really speak of serious mines in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you have talked about surrendering to the JNA. Was there -- what was to be the fate of the Croatian people in Ilok, after the surrender? Was there any discussion about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, as a direct participant in many of these negotiations and in all details, I must tell you that this was not a discussion between equals. On the one hand you have power, a force, an authority, which was arrogant. They simply do not want to respect you as people, as their fellow citizens, until only recently. This was simply a discussion between people who simply did not understand each other. They simply functioned from different positions of power, and, of course, then the negotiations were very difficult, overbearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just interrupting you for a moment, I take it Ilok was predominantly a Croatian town. That is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when the peoples from the other villages came as refugees to the town, most of them were Croatian as well, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of your discussions, and I am talking about the period of 14th/15th October 1991, did discussions relate to the signing of some sort of an agreement between the representatives of your committee, or commission, and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the terms of that agreement in a general sense? I know you cannot probably remember all of it, but what was generally the gist of the agreement that you entered into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection it consists of ten or so articles. There were various groups of subjects involved, and it was agreed that we would be expelled. I must say that under considerable influence of the European Monitors and with their wholehearted support, this agreement was signed on our expulsion from the city of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the expulsion, where was it intended that you would go when you were expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were supposed to go to the then free part of Croatia. There was nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this was to be under the supervision of the JNA and European Monitors, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And that is the way it was carried out, under the supervision of the JNA and European Monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the day before you left Ilok, did you have one final meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you talk to someone intensively, and if you are in touch for about two months -- this was a devastating agreement that we signed, but it was the only way our lives could go on, regardless of how tragic all of this was. You did what you had to do with these people you were negotiating with, and let us say that it was a good deal, and usually, when one concludes a good deal, and when numerous details of this last day were completed and when we all met our obligations, then in the late afternoon hours we wanted to say good bye to people because the next day, according to the agreement, at 7 am the evacuation of the citizens of Ilok began, and we came to a brief farewell meeting with these people with whom we had reached this agreement and with whom we had had these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that this meeting was attended by some people I knew from Backa Palanka. Of course, among them was Mr. Dokmanovic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did the accused -- did Mr. Dokmanovic say to you who he represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My acquaintances from Backa Palanka told me that my president of the municipality was there too, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic and after that, we exchanged a few thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Mr. Dokmanovic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not quite understand what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. When you say Mr. Dokmanovic was at this meeting, on this particular day, this last meeting, did you have a conversation with him, with Mr. Dokmanovic? Did you go up to him and speak to him, or did he approach you and speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked to him. I approached him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you tell us, as best you can recall, what you said to him and what he replied to you in the course of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that during all these negotiations, and even today, I believed that I did not do a thing, and I can say the same of the citizens of Ilok. I mean, in terms of what had happened to them, and that was the subject that I had discussed at the very end when I was tired and exhausted, I asked Slavko, I said, "Slavko, what am I guilty of?", and, "why is it that everything that is happening to me, is happening to me?". That was the question I put then to Slavko and he replied to me that he did not know, that he did not know that, and that he, as the president of the municipality, would establish a people's court and that everyone will be held accountable for the things they are guilty of. After all of that, I had no wish to go into a polemic with Mr. Dokmanovic. I left him with his illusions and his convictions, that some kind of people's courts would be established, and I can just say for sure that then and now I do not know what I have done in order to be in a position to be held accountable by any court, a people's court included.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting, were representatives of the JNA present? At this last meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
