utterances.text: This was their command post, and they were always present there. And one could not even come to the other side of the Danube where they were without having them present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, on the next day, did you and the Croatian people of Ilok leave Ilok and go to Croatian free territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the greatest convoys of expellees in Croatia during this conflict. According to the signed agreement it started at 7 am and the last citizens of Ilok left some time late in the evening, 5 or 6 pm. They left Ilok then, and our estimate has been that this convoy of expellees that included everyone and everything that could move, comprised some 7-10,000 people altogether, this convoy, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And just finally, Mr. Magovac, when you had the meeting, and you met Mr. Dokmanovic where you had the very short conversation with him, are you able to remember what he was wearing at the time? What clothes he had on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never a military person, but in those days people wore some kind of camouflage uniforms in contact with military people. For the first time in my life, then, I saw Mr. Dokmanovic wearing such clothes. This kind of camouflage uniform. I never saw him wearing something like that again -- before that, sorry. He was wearing that kind of attire then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence counsel, you can start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. First of all, in order to correct something we, from Yugoslavia are aware of, are there two separate personalities, two separate persons, the president of the municipality of Vukovar and president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar. Are we talking about one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I do not wish to teach anyone here, and I do not wish to clarify things, but once again, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that I was a professor who was teaching these matters and once again, I have to say that within the local government the lowest level was municipality. Second, a forum for a more immediate expression of people's interest was a local commune. According to the law, local communes could form a so-called community of local communes, and then I draw the attention of the court to the fact that Vukovar did not have that kind of organisation. It did not have a community of local communes. Therefore, at no point did I claim -- it may have been the impression, but I think that I was perfectly clear, there was a municipal assembly, but there was no town assembly of the town of Vukovar. There were assemblies of local communes, and I think you could see it from the transcript, that was the way I explained this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, there is only president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar and not president of the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should have said that right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not intend to correct you, but do you know whether the secretariat for the national defence of the municipal was under the jurisdiction of the JNA or did it belong to the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have a closer look at the law on the national defence, you will see that the concept of national defence -- therefore, the law of the national defence as well -- was based on the idea of armed people. That concept was comprised the elite part, the JNA, and the rest of the population which was armed, which was organised, structured, to the Territorial Defence. The common points they had, and here I am referring to the civilian component to the Territorial Defence, it is very difficult to draw a very precise line, and to say, "the civilian component ends here", and, "the military component starts here", because you know very well that the idea was to have an armed population, armed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but I am not asking you that. Tell me whether the secretariat of the national defence was under the jurisdiction of the JNA or not? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not under the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure, it was the body --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Territorial Defence part of the JNA, or there was a mixture of concepts here as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, we have a law and we will check that out. The elections that took place in 1990, when the municipal assembly of Vukovar was elected and when the accused Dokmanovic was elected president, were those elections multiparty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance on which list was Mr. Dokmanovic? I think he was on the list of the SDP, former Communists. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, you know that there were former Communists among the HDZ as members, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. I will not insist on this particular point. Who was the commander of the MUP Ministry of the Interior in Vukovar in that period? I am referring to the relevant period, 1991, or chief of the Ministry of the Interior for the town of MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chief of MUP, until the incident that took place in Borovo Selo, it was Mr. Zaja and after the Borovo Selo incident and the events that took place there, Mr. Pola became chief of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of function did Mercep have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mercep was the secretary of the secretariat for the national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in May, if I have properly understood you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I confuse the month?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, you did not confuse the month, you confused the accommodation that was provided to the MUP, and the accommodation and food that was provided to the Croatian National Guards. Therefore, accommodation was provided for the MUP and food for the Croatian National Guards. Are you referring to May 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Police forces -- actually one part of police forces due to the existing situation in the town and the municipality, police forces did not have enough local resources, and therefore, in order to maintain law and order of the town, in the town itself, they activated certain units which were outside the town of Vukovar itself. Therefore, these units needed to be provided with proper accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were any Serbs in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened to them? Did they remain in Ilok or did they move out during 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were various approaches by the Serbian population of the town of Ilok. A major part, the majority of Serbs from Ilok have stayed in Ilok, stayed in Ilok until we moved out, and only a small proportion of the local Serbian population left Ilok, and took temporary residence in Backa Palanka and surrounding villages. However, I have to stress that it was a small portion of the Serbian population, but I also have to say that with that small portion of Serbs who had left Ilok, we continued to have contacts in Backa Palanka. We wanted them to come back. We wanted them to share together with us the fate of the town of Ilok and its residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any Croats remain in Ilok when their fellow citizens left, whether there were any citizens that came back, eventually, for example, Vlatko Maric and so on still question, there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some elderly citizens and some other citizens of Ilok, a small part of them, did not wish to leave Ilok at the times we were leaving so they stayed. They remained in the town of Ilok and continued living there, and they lived there throughout all these times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the case with the Slovak population as well? Were there any Slovaks that remained in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Speaking of Slovaks, the majority of the Slovak population stayed in Ilok, and I can only think of some isolated cases left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anything happen to those who stayed behind, Slovaks or Croats, or shall I put it more simply, was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should know that after the 17th October 1991 I was absent from Ilok. I can only tell you what other people told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you know whether anyone has come back, has returned to Ilok while Serbs were still there? Do you know, for example, Vlatko Maric? Did he go back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vlatko Maric did not leave Ilok with the rest of us. He left with his family from Belgrade where his wife, together with her two daughters was staying. I know personally Mr. Maric, and I am very well aware of all the dilemmas he was faced with, and I know that together with his wife, he went back to Ilok from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether the municipal assembly of Vukovar was dissolved at that time and was there a commissioner that was appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that when there is no municipal assembly there is no president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible. Throughout these negotiations you mentioned, negotiations that ended with the signing of the agreement, did you ever see Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic present at those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, you first saw Mr. Dokmanovic after the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did that departure, when you went to say good-bye, was that departure kind of a meeting or was it just an occasion to say good-bye?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we just said, "good-bye".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did that influence in any way your departure? It had already been agreed upon. Did your saying good-bye to him have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Everything by that time, everything had already been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Without the presence of Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, if I am correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were those national people's courts ever established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you that because I was no longer there in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me ask you something in case you remember: the very, "moving-out", that was organised by the JNA in the presence of the international community. There were JNA trucks there, at least that is what I saw on TV in Belgrade. I mean, I was not there, and I trust you, I believe everything you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I am always in favour of a good dialogue, but I have to say that under the pressure of the representatives whose role has not been emphasised enough, representatives of the international community, I can say that there were real professionals, and good people, and they forced the JNA to behave in a proper way and to respect what had been agreed upon in the agreement. They fulfilled their obligation from the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When the JNA was involved in that, when everything -- when that was actually taking place, was there anyone from Serbia there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the control of the town of Ilok? Was that the JNA or civilian authorities? Who, for example, controlled people who were leaving Ilok? Police or the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the military, but it was in the presence of, as a kind of moral support, in the presence of citizens of Serbian nationality. And this is where our human dignity was offended at that moment, by their very presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I fully understand you, if it means anything to you. Do you know who was in charge of appointing directors of various companies in the town of Ilok later on? Was that the military or civilian authorities? Who was in charge of resettlement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and because I was not present there at that period, I can only speak about what I have learned. I am not speaking through my direct knowledge, so according to the information I have, at that time, in Ilok, first of all there were some two days, 48 hours of total chaos. There was no proper authority. After that period of time, after those 48 hours, some kind of civilian authority was established in Ilok, but those were not residents of the town of Ilok, but some -- but people who had come from elsewhere. As for the political structure, and the organisation of the authority, speaking of all other bodies and factions, I think that the situation was completely unclear, and that it was not possible to define it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that Ljubo Novakovic suggested to you that the two of you should negotiate with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, just one more question in order to clarify things. Did the JNA attack or carry out any kind of military operation on the town of Ilok, and here I am referring to possible attempts of disarming paramilitary units, and so on, the way it happened in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot compare the situation with what happened in Vukovar. You know, what happened in Vukovar is something completely different and it is completely beyond comparison, so that is the first question. I cannot compare Vukovar and Ilok, because it did not happen the same way. However, I have to state here clearly and with full responsibility that first of all, whether there was an attack or not, it is difficult for me to say, because I am by no means a military expert and I was never involved in military matters. I do not know whether shooting incidents -- restriction of free movement, for example; I myself could not go to my vineyards because the JNA was on the road, and so on. I am here mentioning many details, but if -- I have to give you a clear answer as to the attack, then I have to say that no such attack took place, I mean no destruction took place. However, there were numerous shooting incidents, there was a lot of provocation, the citizens were exposed to psychological pressure and so on. It is very easy to speak about that situation here from this perspective, from the courtroom where both Mr. Dokmanovic and I are sitting today. It was completely different thing, the situation that took place on the 15th October 1991 was completely different, and if you ask me to draw a parallel to compare Ilok and Vukovar, then I can say that there was no attack in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I turn to the Prosecutor, and ask him how much time he needs for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I need no time, your Honour. I am not going to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So therefore, we -- is there any objection to the witness being released? (Pause). No? Right. So you may be released, and thank you for coming. (The witness withdrew) Before we stand in recess, may I ask both parties whether they could be so kind as to provide to the court 1) the relevant legislation regulating the functioning of the various bodies in the municipalities in the former Yugoslavia. We would like to get this and to go through the relevant legislation; 2) the relevant legislation on national defence system; and 3) if possible, I do not know whether there is any written text of the agreement which has been referred to, the agreement about the evacuation of people from Ilok. Is there a written text of this agreement? If so, could we get a copy of this written document? Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect to the country that I am going back to, I hope that neither you nor Mr. Niemann do not have such a difficult army in any one of your countries, getting something from them is awful. But I am giving you my word, I will do my best. I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would think that we have very little chance of getting that information, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Anyway, let us try. Thank you. So we now stand in recess for -- Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry, I will provide the laws for you, that is no problem whatsoever, as far as the laws are concerned, perhaps it is a bit of misunderstanding. Yes, I am going to get you the laws, I think you even have them, but the agreement is a problem. You see, in the evidence, material, provided by the Prosecutor, it was said that the military made lists. I did not manage to get these lists. It was mentioned that they made videotapes. They will not let us get copies of them. That is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we stand in recess for fifteen minutes. Not more than fifteen minutes. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness comes in I regret I misspoke just prior to the adjournment. We do, in fact, have the agreement, but it has not been translated, so we will have to go through the process of having it translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Wonderful. Thank you. That is very good news.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might indicate, your Honour, we will be calling a witness later on who actually signed the agreement, so we can show you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. While we are waiting for the witness, may I, to avoid wasting time, tell you -- say a few words about the hearings which we are resuming on 2nd February ? To my regret, we will only have eight working days available because the 12th -- on 12th February our courtroom is needed for two different cases, Kovacevic and Furundzija and for the 15th for the Celebici case. Now, to make up for this, the shortening of our period, I suggested to our Registry that we should start every day at 9 o'clock. You know that we will have full days, but I am afraid this is impossible, so therefore, now, the Registry told me this morning that we may start at 9.15, and stop at 1 o'clock, resume at 2.30 until 5.30 in the afternoon. This is the maximum which is possible, because of logistics and financial implications, and so on. So this will apply, therefore, this timetable will apply to the first five working days from 2nd-6th February, and then to the 9th -- from the 9th to the 11th. So I hope that in the light of that the Prosecutor may make the necessary preparation for the witnesses. I wonder whether we could receive from the Prosecutor maybe a few days before -- you said on the Thursday prior to 2nd February, a list of the witnesses you intend to call for the following week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And, of course, the Defence as well. Thank you. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Waespi will take the next witness, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness will make the formal declaration. MARINKO VLADIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You feel comfortable? Can we start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Will you please state to the court your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marinko Vladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the place and date of your birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Ilok on 2nd December 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please state your nationality and your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Croatian national of Croatian ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please outline shortly your educational background, which schools did you attend from high school on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the agricultural faculty in Zagreb. I completed my secondary education in Ilok and I studied and graduated in Sarajevo, at the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you finish, and with what degree did you finish, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I obtained my degree in 1984, and I am an ergonomics engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you serve in the JNA, and for how long was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in the JNA for ten months and twenty six days exactly in 1984 and 1985 and I was based in Stip in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any experience in your profession, in your civil profession after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not fully understand your question. What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: After you completed your studies in Sarajevo you started your work, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of employment was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I came back from the army I was unemployed for about a year, and then in 1986 I was employed by the Zupic company. I was an intern for one year. I had to do my internship in Ilok and Vukovar and after the internship I stayed for two years in Vukovar Wine Cellars Company, so after two years spent in Vukovar Wine Cellars Company I returned to Ilok and I worked in Ilok until 17th October 1991, and I still occupy the same post as I had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Therefore, since 1989 your workplace has always been Ilok. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that you always lived in Ilok, the same place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Even when I worked in Vukovar I used to commute from Ilok every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Ilok, the town you were living in, and you also worked in, was part of the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before the war, what was the approximate population and the ethnic composition of the town of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, approximately, there were about 7,000 inhabitants in Ilok. There were about 500 Serbs, 2,500 Slovaks, and about 4,000 Croats. That is just ballpark figure, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. In the surroundings of Ilok there were some neighbouring villages. Can you name us some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area between Vukovar and Ilok there were several villages, Sotin, Opatovac, Mohovo, Sarengrad. They were situated alongside the main road to Vukovar. They were also villages of Bapska, and Tovarnik. The majority of the population was of Croat origin in those villages. Therefore, the area between Vukovar and Ilok had the majority of Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Turning now to the events in summer 1991, you just said a moment ago that you, at that time, were living and working in Ilok. How was the company called you were employed with? I think you might have mentioned the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vupik. The name of the company was Vupik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In what position were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I was chief of the financial section of the Ilok Wine Cellars Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Vladic, can you describe to the court the situation in late summer of 1991? First of all, is it correct to say that you were a member of the local crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was your role in this body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was the president of the civilian protection department, and in that sense I was charged with taking care of civilians, providing accommodation, water supplies, food and so on. In case of shelling, I was also in charge of transferring these people to shelters and so on. We had civil engineers as well in case of major destruction. These people were supposed to evacuate the wounded, and I also had a role to play in a potential evacuation of the population. Therefore, because I knew some people who had trucks and so on, in case of evacuation we were supposed to be prepared for that. At that time the town was surrounded, encircled, and we are speaking about the end of October 1991, so between the 10th and the 17th of October the town was already under a blockade, and the residents of the surrounding villages were fleeing, and arriving in great numbers in Ilok. The population, therefore, almost doubled. The roads were blocked, and in view of the situation we had nothing else but to try and attempt a breakthrough. On 17th October we all left the town of Ilok in a convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "we all left"? How many people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not all of us left, it is true. Some people remained, but it is my estimate that between 12 and 13,000 people left the town. Elderly people mostly stayed. My parents also stayed in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the population was about 7,000 and you said that it almost doubled because of people who were fleeing into -- and of those you are just saying that maybe 12 and 13,000 people left the town on 17th October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So on that day it was a huge convoy getting out of the town, on October 17th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any ultimatum from the part of the JNA issued at the people of Ilok? You were part of it a short time before you left on October 17th. Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no ultimatum for us to leave the town, but the town was encircled. Nobody actually told us to leave the town, but since it was surrounded, it was the military who had the control over the electricity supply and the water supply. The population, as I said, doubled, and we could hear explosions coming from afar, coming from the area of Vukovar, and some people already knew that there had been a number of murders, killings and so on. So these people kept coming to the town, and in that situation, the only way out was the way out of town. But since it was under a blockade we could not leave the town without the permission of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did the people of Ilok convene into a meeting, an assembly, at a certain point prior to leaving in order to discuss these kinds of -- urge of the JNA to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The residents of the town were in their houses at their homes and on 17th, when the convoy was organised, people simply started leaving the town. A lot of people had -- were hesitating, but once it started, everybody left. I was also surprised when I realised how many people had gathered, in the meantime, in Ilok. There was a great number of vehicles, tractors, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Turning back, now, to this very event on 17th October, did you have any guarantees from the army which, as you have said before, completely blocked the town that you could leave, that nothing would happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have that, yes. They did guarantee that nothing would happen to us, but there were also European Monitors there, people dressed in white uniforms, and they were also some kind of guarantee that nothing would happen to us, although personally I was not quite sure, and the situation for us was very unsafe and insecure, in spite of the fact that we were told that nothing would happen, that we were allowed to leave. We lived in fear, because we did not know what could happen, whether we could actually leave the town or not. People were faced with a major dilemma. Some people did not want to join the convoy but attempted to break through on their own, but that was a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you part of any team of negotiations within the town of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning, now, to your personal role, which route did you take to get out of the town? Can you describe that in a little bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The route was agreed upon in advance. We could not choose. We left Ilok in the direction of the bridge connecting banks of the Danube. Backa Palanka was on the other side and there was a checkpoint on this side where papers and vehicles were controlled, and from that point on we continued in the direction of Sid. Do you want me to continue with the details?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Were you stopped at one moment around this bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere near the bridge. There was a checkpoint, and I was behind the wheel of a Golf, and was stopped by a man in uniform. I thought he was an officer. I do not think he was just a simple soldier, so I showed him my documents and documents of the vehicle, and he told me that I was allowed to go, but that I could not take the car, and he also found my name on the list of members of the crisis committee and I told him that indeed I was a member of the crisis committee, and president of -- and he told me that I could go, but that I had to leave the car. That was a very difficult situation for me. Vehicles were all loaded and packed and I was afraid that I would not have any means of transport to cross over, and at that point, standing some 50 metres away, I saw Slavko Dokmanovic and president of the Backa Palanka municipality, Ljubo Novakovic, and I asked them for help. I approached them and I wanted to introduce myself because I was not sure whether they knew me or not. So as I was about to introduce myself, Slavko said, "yes, I know you. Just tell me what you want", and I told him that I was driving our vehicle, because Slavko also worked in the Vupik company but he said that I could leave but I could not take the car because the car was company property. And then I said that he should send a soldier with me to the border and that then the soldier could take back the car, but he still refused, and at that moment Ljubo Novakovic told me that I could, that I was allowed to stay in Ilok if I did not have blood on my hands. At that moment I really felt sick. I thought I was going to faint, and I said that. At that moment Slavko brought some fruit juice to me, and after I drank that I was feeling a bit better, so I went to the vehicle and I started unloading it, and at that moment, chief of the Ilok police arrived and I told him that they wanted to take the vehicle, and then he talked to a JNA officer, and the officer asked me whose vehicle it was, and I said that it was a company car, and he asked me, "why are you driving it?". I told him that I was the manager of a department of the company and I showed him my card, so he took the card, he read it and gave it back to me and he said that I could take the car. So I went back to the car and that is how I crossed over to the other side. But I must say that after we passed the checkpoint I was still afraid that I would be stopped again, that they would tell me that I was not allowed to drive that vehicle. That lasted for about half an hour until I reached the territory which was under the control of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vladic. You just described having seen Mr. Dokmanovic in Ilok on October 17th 1991. Can you tell us, what clothes did he wear at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing a camouflage uniform. A military uniform that was usually worn by the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Having described Mr. Dokmanovic, how many times did you see him before that event, before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war I saw him several times, not many times, but just a couple of times. I think I met him in the Vukovar Wine Cellars Company. At that time he was the president of the workers' council, and I was at that time also a member of the workers' council and I was present at the meeting that he chaired at that time. So that was, for example, one of the occasions. We were not real acquaintances but I knew him and I assumed that he knew me, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And besides being the president of that same company you worked with, or the president of the workers' council, I have to specify, what official role did Mr. Dokmanovic have in the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the president of the municipality, president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you see Mr. Dokmanovic today in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I recognised him right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that you saw, besides Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Novakovic, and you described him as being the president of the municipal assembly of Backa Palanka. Can you describe to the court today the way Mr. Novakovic was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic was wearing civilian clothes. He had a blazer on. That is all, more or less, I can remember. I just know that he was wearing civilian clothes. I cannot remember the details, but I know that he was dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Coming back to Mr. Dokmanovic and you on that day, can you tell us the way you perceived his presence, his appearance? What did he look to you at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the moment when the officer who was standing in the checkpoint told me that I was not allowed to drive the car. It was at that moment that I requested that I wanted to ask him for some help. I saw Slavko and I could see on his face that he was worried, although he refused when I asked for help, he said that, "you could not drive the car. You can leave but you cannot take the car", but as I say, I could see that he was worried, but when I explained to him what the problem was, he did not want to help me. I even said that when I felt that I was going to faint, as I told you, he even brought me some juice, but as far as help is concerned, he refused. He said, "no". He was wearing a military uniform, a camouflage military uniform. That is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You said to us that he was worried. In your opinion, what was he worried about, in this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably because of this huge number of people. It was a horrible picture. It was a very long convoy, lots of people, elderly, young, vehicles, cars, tractors, everything was moving in the direction of Sid and Croatia. I think it was a horrible image, and no man could stand there and simply observe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your personal experience on that very day, did it appear to you that Mr. Dokmanovic was part of the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was the president of the municipality. Well, I must say that at that moment I did not think about that, in these terms. I simply saw him standing there and I wanted to ask him for help. For me he was an acquaintance from my company. He was the president of the municipality and I thought that he might be able to help me because I saw some other people standing there in uniforms, people from Ilok, but it did not occur to me to ask them for help because I knew that they could not help me. That is why I approached Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for the record, at least a visual one in the courtroom, can you point out the accused, Mr. Dokmanovic? Just with your arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he is sitting over there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Do you know that Mr. Dokmanovic, who was president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar, do you know that this assembly was dissolved by a decision of the Croat authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that -- well, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you do not remember then do you not have to say anything. It is not that important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that Marin Vidic-Bili was involved, but literally that someone had dissolved something or fired someone, I do not know, and I did not have enough time to think about it at that point. I found out about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That the assembly was dissolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that the assembly was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, at the point when you met Slavko Dokmanovic, was he president of the Vukovar municipal assembly or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point I did not have time to think about that at all. I saw a man, and I thought that he could help me and that is why I addressed him. Whether someone was president of the municipality or whatever, that point I did not give it any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I know you did not give it any thought and no normal person would. I mean, your family in the car and everything, of course, I fully understand that. Later on, did you find out that the municipal assembly of Vukovar was dissolved and that he was no longer president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found that out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So at that point you did not know that he was president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the city, the town of Ilok have its own municipal assembly and its president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilok was not a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But did it have a president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not a municipality. It was within the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what were Ivan Mr.sic and Crvenkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- well, he was the mayor of Ilok at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So Ilok was a town, right, so it had a mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And Crvenkovic. But Ilok was still within the municipality of Vukovar, right, and Crvenkovic, was he president of the executive board, Crvenkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I know that he was in the local government, but I do not know whether he was president of the executive council or whatever. I really do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. In 1991, before you got out of Ilok, did the entire Serb population leave or part of the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the Serb population left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did some of the people who left with you, part of the Croat population, did they come back after some time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But there were such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only some people, maybe three, four, five people at a maximum. That is to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you left Ilok, did you go through Serb territory and then go to Croat territory again and were you attacked by someone then, the JNA? Were you beaten up by someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you pass safely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So could one draw the conclusion that the JNA had kept its promise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I mean in relation to security and safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I speak now? I did leave safely and no one attacked me, but some 30 people were taken out of the convoy and to camps in Serbia, but I left safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know about this, but if you say so, I imagine it is true. And, because you said some time ago that the JNA did not present you with an ultimatum, was there a referendum, conditionally speaking, that was carried out among the population of Ilok, whether Ilok should be abandoned or whether people should leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what was the result of this referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult for me to say that it was a referendum. It was a way in which people declared themselves when the town was surrounded by tanks, armour and armed soldiers. In that situation, in order to get out of town we would have signed anything, just to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but did someone come and force you to leave? Did you have to come out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this question is quite unclear to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For example, did the accused Dokmanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, the city was surrounded. There was shooting from Vukovar and from the surrounding villages. You could hear explosions all the time. There was a war going on, you know, and in that situation you ask me whether someone had forced me to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you want me to clarify the question? Personally, for example, Slavko Dokmanovic who you see here, did he force you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he personally did not force me to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your stay in Ilok, until you left Ilok, did you see Slavko Dokmanovic getting in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On what side did you talk to him? On the Serbian side or the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: By the checkpoint, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the JNA checkpoint, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you felt ill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you feel ill because of what Dokmanovic said or what Ljubo Novakovic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to distinguish between the two. Yes. It is hard to distinguish between the two. This was a very short conversation. I came there, and I wanted to take the car and he told me that I could not take the car and Ljubo said, "you can stay here if you have no blood on your hands", and at that point in time I felt faint and I imagine that Slavko saw it on my face that I would pass out and he brought me a juice and then I felt better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when Slavko Dokmanovic brought you this juice did you take this as aggression or did you take this as help by a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think such a question is pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I guess it is not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, he helped me at that point. No doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And a lot of people ask you, "how did you experience this?", and, "how did you experience that?", so how did you experience the fact that he brought you a glass of juice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that and I want to highlight that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that he did not have any insignia of rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that he did not have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you still abide by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened to the car that you had set out with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took the car to Zagreb and I handed it over to the company where I was employed. We had a representative office of Vupik in Zagreb so I handed it over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the car remained in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So now this car is in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where it is supposed to be, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Re-examination? (Pause). I have two questions. Now, you said that there was no ultimatum issued by JNA to the population in Ilok. That means -- and you also, I understand, you added that the population there was not physically or militarily forced to leave the town; my question is whether there was any psychological pressure by the JNA. What is your view? Do you think that there was any, say, formal threat implicit in various actions, or in the conduct of the JNA, any form of constraint, or did the population leave simply out of fear that, say, the fighting might also erupt in the town so that people would be wounded, killed, and so on. Could you answer this question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town was encircled, as I said. It was under blockade. I am an ergonomist. I also worked as an anologist. We could not have people out in the vineyards. We could not even pick the grapes, because we were afraid that there would be fighting within the town itself and we were afraid that if we would not leave, the people would lose their lives, there would be a lot of destruction, so we did our very best to get out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right, but so there was no formal threat or any form of threat by the JNA? No sort of incentive or inducement to the population to go out of the town, to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were not special incentives, and no one made us leave. We ordinary citizens did not have any special contacts with the army. They had deployed tanks and cannons at certain points. For example, from my bathroom window I could see all this artillery facing the town. At night there was shooting. They shot at the town, and you could hear explosions from Vukovar, and no one could get out of town or get into town. No one would come and tell us something or threaten us, saying that they would do this and that if we would not leave, but the atmosphere was such that every person wanted to get out of such a place. Under such circumstances we had this referendum carried out and we said that we wanted to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then, I mean, how do you explain that, if I understood you correctly, actually most Croats left the town, and whereas most Serbs remained in the town, only a few of them left the town. How do you explain this difference in behaviour? Normally in a town, surrounded by military -- by an army, and by tanks and so on, normally the whole population, except probably for the wounded, the elderly, would leave the town. How do you explain this difference in -- based on the ethnic origin of the various segments of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, we all knew that the JNA, although it was called, "The Yugoslavia People's Army", we knew that the people who were in uniform and under whose control these tanks and cannons and whatever were, were of Serb ethnic origin and I imagine that we were more fearful than the Serbs, although quite a few Serbs had left with us too. However, part of the Serbs had left before this date of October 17th, because they were going towards Backa Palanka and Sid. They were allowed to pass, and four, five or six days before 17th the town was completely sealed off so no one could get in or out. Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore, on 17th October, you said that, roughly speaking, between 12 and 13,000 people left Ilok. Roughly speaking, again, now, how many of those 12 or 13,000 people were Serbs? It is very difficult to say, I know, but I mean, have you got an idea or are you in a position to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps about 100, about 100, not very many of them, I think, because in the convoy there were people from the surrounding villages, not only from Ilok. I mean, the villages between Ilok and Vukovar. These people had come to Ilok before, and then they were leaving Ilok together with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my second question is about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just after you have finished, may I ask for an additional question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On this very point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Probably it is better for you to step in now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said, just answering that, "no incentives", you are not aware of any incentives that was given by the JNA to people from Ilok. You were not part of those negotiations, you said, in testimony with the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not take part in the negotiations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there might be incentives but not issued to, or communicated to you personally? You just do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You see, there was a commission, a certain group of people who went to these negotiations, and what they talked about with the army I do not know, and I do not want to go into that, and I do not want to give any kind of assessment as to what they were saying there. After the several meetings they had we were told that we were supposed to have a referendum carried out where we would decide whether we would get out of town or not and we decided to get out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your kindness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you help me with something? I just want to be plain; there is no dispute that Mr. Dokmanovic was on the bridge. Is that right? That is not disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I may move on to my second question, you said, Mr. Vladic, you said that you saw the accused wearing a camouflage -- I am reading what you said -- camouflage uniform, usually worn by JNA soldiers. Was it common for civilians to wear -- in Ilok -- camouflage uniforms? Because at some point you also said, "other people from Ilok were wearing uniforms", so how many of those people you were referring to in the sentence I have just quoted, how many of them were civilians? Was it a normal daily occurrence that some civilians would wear military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, there was a war going on, so there were some people in Ilok who had camouflaged uniforms but not the kind that Slavko had. It was a shade different from the uniforms that Croats wore in Ilok too. There were also some armed people in Ilok who walked around in uniform. So it is very difficult for me to answer this question. There was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but what is the difference between these two types of uniforms? You said other people were wearing a different sort of uniform from the one worn by Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They differ. These are camouflage uniforms but they are different from one another. For example, the colours are not exactly the same shade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But then at one point you said that the uniform Mr. Dokmanovic was wearing is the one usually worn by JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And whereas the other uniforms you saw, the other people in uniform you saw in Ilok, may be some of them being civilians, did not wear that particular type of uniform. This is what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Croats in Ilok, some Croats, also wore camouflaged uniformed but not the kind that Slavko had. Also camouflage uniforms, but quite different, of a different colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In connection to the witness, I do not have any further questions, but I may perhaps assist the court. In response to Judge May's question, I said that Slavko was at the bridge. Kindly see a videotape of the conversation between Mr. Milner and Mr. Druzo with Mr. Dokmanovic here in the prison, and then you will see why he was there at the bridge with Ljubo Novakovic. If you are interested in that, the tapes are held by the gentleman from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecution has any more questions. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore there is no objection to Mr. Vladic being released, no objection. So, Mr. Vladic, you may be released. Thank you so much for coming. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn is there any question to be raised? Any comment about our hearings on the 2nd? We will resume our hearings, as I said before, on 2nd February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. That is all the witnesses we have brought today, so that is the last witness for the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: By the way, I asked you whether you could be so kind, and you accepted my suggestion, so kind as to provide us with a list of witnesses. I wonder whether you could also specify for each witness the estimated length of examination-in-chief? I know that it is a very rough estimate, of course. I know, I agree with you that it is very difficult, but still, if we could have a rough idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will see what we can do, your Honours. We will have a better idea after we speak to them and they probably will not be here the Thursday before. They generally do not arrive until the Saturday, so we do not see them, so it may be a bit inaccurate, but we can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On Monday, could you give it to us on Monday, so we could get from you on maybe, Thursday, the list of witnesses and on Monday the list of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So the hearing -- yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. I did not understand you personally, what you were saying. Am I supposed to give a list of witnesses too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood what you were saying. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, it was only for the Prosecutor. Then, the hearing stands adjourned. (12.30 pm)
